newsitem.title: USA: IPAA suggests in-kind U.S. oil royalties system.
newsitem.headline: IPAA suggests in-kind U.S. oil royalties system.

text.p: Independent oil producers are pushing for the U.S. Minerals Management Service to change to a system of in-kind payments of federal oil royalties.
The Independent Petroleum Association of America wants the MMS to drop its proposal to base royalties calculations on crude oil futures and Alaska North Slope crude prices.
Instead, the IPAA said MMS should take the payments in oil, which it would sell at the best possible prices.
"This is being done in Canada very effectively and we feel this should be the MMS' primary goal," the IPAA said in recommendations released at its annual meeting.

Until the MMS is ready to switch to in-kind payments, the IPAA said the agency should "fundamentally revise" its existing system to ensure that royalty payments from arm's length sales are at or near the lease where the oil production occured.
Gross proceeds received would represent true market value from which royalty payments can be calculated, the IPPA said.

For non-arm's length sales, the IPAA proposed changing the current system to better ensure proper valuation. References to "posted prices" should be removed, and all royalties should be based on comparable market value lease transactions at or near the lease, the IPAA said.

The IPAA said the MMS should not restrict arm's length transactions at the lease. "Any basis for MMS' proposals regarding companies who purchase oil and companies whose production is subject to crude oil calls should be looked at individually," it said.
It also said the MMS should abandon a proposal to impose on lease holders a new duty to to assume all crude oil marketing expenses downstream from the lease at no cost to the federal lessor.
"The proposed duty is a breach of faith with lessees based on a complete misunderstanding of the lessee's duty to put crude oil into marketable condition," the IPAA said.
The MMS has twice extended the public comment period on its royalties proposal. The comment period ends May 28, but the agency said it could reopen that.
Oil companies have complained that they might end up overpaying royalties under the MMS proposal to base royalties on crude oil futures prices and ANS prices.
